passage:
At sixteen, Devika had a history project due in three weeks, and she opened the file every evening and closed it again. If she started, she might discover she could not do it well. So she reorganised her shelves, watched two episodes of a show and told herself, "I work better under pressure." Her teacher Samir asked how it was going. "Fine," she said.

Four years later, in college, a paper was due at nine the next morning. At six in the evening Devika began, and fear turned to energy. She wrote through the night with coffee and her friend Rafiq's notes, and submitted at dawn. The grade was decent. "See?" she said to Rafiq, bleary-eyed. "Last minute works."

Two days later she caught a cold from exhaustion and missed the next class. She noticed, without saying it aloud, that she had got a lower mark than Rafiq, who had started a week early and had gone out to dinner the night before.

qa.q: At what time on the deadline day did Devika begin her college paper?
qa.a: Devika began at six in the evening.

qa.q: How are the delay at sixteen and the all-night sprint at twenty connected?
qa.a: At sixteen Devika avoids starting because a poor result would expose weakness, and at twenty the same delay ends in a panic sprint that works well enough to teach her that last minute is fine, although the cost is exhaustion and a lower mark than Rafiq.

qa.q: What was Devika probably feeling as she opened and closed the file every evening at sixteen?
qa.a: Devika was afraid of doing badly, so she protected her self-image by not starting.

qa.q: What could Devika try before the next deadline?
qa.a: She could start with a small, rough section early and ask for feedback, so fear of a poor result does not keep her waiting for panic.

grounding: Procrastination linked across ages: a teenager avoiding a project to protect her self-image, and the later panic sprint that seems to work but carries a cost.
